newsitem.title: USA: Union says Kennecott strike raises Chino tensions.
newsitem.headline: Union says Kennecott strike raises Chino tensions.

text.p: The strike at Kennecott Utah Copper has raised tensions at Phelps Dodge Corp's Chino mine where workers have been without labor contracts for over three months, a United Steelworkers of America official said.
"There are a lot of things that can have a direct impact on Phelps Dodge with this walkout," USWA lead negotiator at Chino, Robert Guadiana said.
Phelps spokeswoman Sue Suver said output at Chino was unaffected and on target to reach planned 1996 projections.
"We are not seeing disruption to our production there as a result of how employees are feeling. The mine product is not being impacted. There is a message there," Suver said.
Some 1,800 workers at Kennecott, largely represented by USWA, walked out on Wednesday. The plant is being operated by management at a reduced level of production, the company said.
At Phelps Dodge's Chino 170,000 tonnes per year of contained copper mine in New Mexico some 670 unionised employees have been working without contract since midnight June 30.
Guadiana said he was in contact with USWA leaders at Kennecott.

Kennecott has offered a pay rise, while Phelps has said a four-year pay freeze was its final offer. "Our people should not be expected to take less," Guadiana said. "But they are both being unfair to their workforce."
The Kennecott strike heightened tensions at Chino and presented "interesting possibility of any action" at the New Mexico mine, Guadiana said.
Chino labor unions and management resume talks on October 24 and 25 in Las Cruces, New Mexico, Guadiana said.
"There are a lot of disgruntled workers out there," Guadiana said of Chino. "It's probably at the height of adversarial relations they have ever had there."
Worker grievances have led to some production losses at Chino's mine and solvent extraction plant, Guadiana claimed.
"I do know that they are down dramatically in their production," Guadiana said. "I have heard of numbers from 25 to 50 percent...and that's from management."
